newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW - China toll roads seen crowding IPO mkt.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - China toll roads seen crowding IPO mkt.

text.p: Inspired by the success of GZI Transport Ltd's IPO, Chinese highway operators are rushing to list shares in Hong Kong, hoping to take advantage of recent interest in China infrastructure stocks, analysts said.
At least six China toll road companies are planning to either offer H-shares or float as "red chips" in the first half of 1997, market sources said.
Red chips are stocks of Hong Kong-based firms with strong Chinese ties, while H-shares are stocks of mainland China-incorporated companies listed in Hong Kong.
"They want to just copy the GZI story," one source said.
Last month's initial public offering (IPO) of shares in GZI Transport, an infrastructure spinoff of Guangzhou Investment Co Ltd, was more than 500 times oversubscribed.
The stock closed nearly 51 percent above its issue price on the first day of trading.
Alan Kasket, investment analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said Chinese demand for new roads was expected to increase.
"In developed countries, look at the trend, you will see that people prefer to use roads over other means of transport," he said.
China is expected to need US$65 billion for road construction in the next five years but will be able to come up with only 15-25 percent of that, the Xinhua news agency said in December.
China hopes to tap overseas stock markets for the rest.
Analysts said China infrastructure companies such as road operators, which have relatively stable incomes, were the latest favourites in the IPO market. But the euphoria may not last.
"The increasing supply will add pressure on the existing and upcoming highway stocks," said Michael Ng, an analyst at ASG Investment.
Kasket said investors were also becoming selective in picking China-based stocks. "They are far more sort of seeking out stocks which have particular value."
"We will have to look very closely at the assets that each company is offering," he said.
But one local fund manager said existing roads were not expected to generate exciting revenue growth for their companies.
"The major concern will be whether they are able to get hold of quality projects at a good discount to asset values in the future," he said.
ASG's Ng also said "guanxi", which is Mandarin for "connections", would determine success.
"A good 'guanxi' is especially important in China as tolls and other conditions of the roads are very much dependent on the management's relationship with the government," he said.
Kasket said such connections would be advantageous only if they could be translated into hard currency through tax breaks or guaranteed income from authorities.
Not every Chinese road operator has had a successful float.

Shares of Road King Infrastructure Ltd, a China highway spinoff of civil engineering group Wai Kee Holdings Ltd, have traded below their offer price of HK$8.40 since their stock market debut in July 1996.
But analysts said road operators planning H-share listings have direct connections with Chinese transport authorities through majority shareholdings.
Shenzhen Expressway Co is seeking an H-share listing in March with an offering of 650 million shares. The issue is expected to raise up to HK$1.58 billion, market sources said.
The offering is expected to be followed by Jiangsu Ninghu Expressway Co Ltd, Zhejiang Hangyong Expressway Co Ltd, and Chengyu Expressway Co Ltd, they said.
